questions.prompt: Let \(B=\big((1,1),(1,-1)\big)\). Find the matrix \(P\) from B-coordinates to standard coordinates.
questions.answer: The columns of \(P\) are the basis vectors of \(B\) written in standard coordinates. Therefore \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). This matrix sends \([v]_B\) to the standard coordinate vector \(v\).

questions.prompt: Using \(B=\big((1,1),(1,-1)\big)\), convert B-coordinates \((2,1)\) to standard coordinates.
questions.answer: The coordinate vector \((2,1)\) means \(v=2(1,1)+1(1,-1)\). Compute \(2(1,1)=(2,2)\), then add \((1,-1)\) to get \((3,1)\). Therefore the standard coordinates are \((3,1)\).
Solve \(a(1,1)+b(1,-1)=(3,1)\). This gives \(a+b=3\) and \(a-b=1\). Adding equations gives \(2a=4\), so \(a=2\). Then \(b=1\). Therefore \([v]_B=(2,1)\).

questions.prompt: Let \(B=\big((2,0),(0,3)\big)\). Find \(P\) from B-coordinates to standard coordinates and \(P^{-1}\).
questions.answer: The basis matrix is \(P=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). It sends \((a,b)\) to \((2a,3b)\). The inverse sends \((x,y)\) to \((x/2, y/3)\), so \(P^{-1}\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\0&1/3\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Convert standard coordinates \((10,12)\) to B-coordinates for \(B=\big((2,0),(0,3)\big)\).
questions.answer: We need \(a(2,0)+b(0,3)=(10,12)\). This gives \(2a=10\) and \(3b=12\). Hence \(a=5\) and \(b=4\). Therefore the B-coordinates are \((5,4)\).

questions.prompt: For \(B=\big((1,0),(1,1)\big)\), find the standard vector represented by B-coordinate vector \((3,-2)\).

questions.answer: Solve \(a(1,0)+b(1,1)=(1,-2)\). This gives \((a+b,b)=(1,-2)\). From the second component, \(b=-2\). Then \(a+b=1\) gives \(a-2=1\), so \(a=3\). Therefore \([v]_B=(3,-2)\).

questions.prompt: Explain why a change-of-basis matrix must be invertible.
questions.answer: A change-of-basis matrix has basis vectors as columns. Basis vectors are linearly independent and span the space. Therefore the matrix has independent columns and a pivot in every column, so it is invertible. Invertibility is necessary because changing coordinates must be reversible.

questions.prompt: Let \(B=\big(1+x,1-x\big)\). Convert B-coordinates \((2,1)\) to a polynomial in \(P_1\).
questions.answer: The coordinate vector \((2,1)\) means \(p=2(1+x)+1(1-x)\). Expanding gives \(2+2x+1-x=3+x\). Therefore the polynomial is \(3+x\).

questions.prompt: A learner says changing basis changes the vector itself. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Changing basis changes the coordinate description of a vector, not the vector itself. For example, the vector \((3,1)\) has standard coordinates \((3,1)\), but in the basis \(\big((1,1),(1,-1)\big)\) it has coordinates \((2,1)\). Both coordinate lists describe the same vector. The learner confused the vector with its coordinates.
